This document outlines the testing 
 procedure P1, which must be performed 
 on an monthly basis as indicated by M1 in the above title 
 block

The main sources of dissolved oxygen in 
 water are the atmospheric oxygen and the oxygen produced from photo process by the algae.

The solubility of atmospheric oxygen in fresh 
 waters ranges from 14.6 mg/L at 0 oC to about 7mg/L at 35oC 
 under 1 atmosphere pressure.

Dissolved oxygen measurements are vital for maintaining aerobic conditions 
in natural waters that receive pollutional matter and in aerobic treatment 
processes intended to purify domestic and industrial waste waters.

Dissolved oxygen determinations are used for the maintenance of dissolved oxygen 
levels that will support the desired aquatic life in a healthy condition at all 
times.
Determinations of dissolved oxygen serve as the basis of the BOD test.

text:
Title
Standard Test Method for Dissolved Oxygen in water
Introduction
This document outlines the testing 
 procedure P1, which must be performed 
 on an monthly basis as indicated by M1 in the above title 
 block
The main sources of dissolved oxygen in 
 water are the atmospheric oxygen and the oxygen produced from photo process by the algae.
The solubility of atmospheric oxygen in fresh 
 waters ranges from 14.6 mg/L at 0 oC to about 7mg/L at 35oC 
 under 1 atmosphere pressure.
Significance
Dissolved oxygen measurements are vital for maintaining aerobic conditions 
in natural waters that receive pollutional matter and in aerobic treatment 
processes intended to purify domestic and industrial waste waters.
Dissolved oxygen determinations are used for the maintenance of dissolved oxygen 
levels that will support the desired aquatic life in a healthy condition at all 
times.
Determinations of dissolved oxygen serve as the basis of the BOD test.
Sampling
Samples must 
 overflow two or three times the volume 
 of 
 the bottles to ensure collection of representative 
 samples. Most samples for dissolved oxygen are collected in the field where it 
 is not convenient to perform the entire determination, it is customary to 
 'fix' the samples immediately after collection.
Methods of Determining Dissolved Oxygen
The winkler or iodometric methods and its modification are the standard 
volumetric procedures for determining dissolved oxygen at the present time, the 
test depends upon that oxygen oxidizes Mn++ 
to a higher state of valence under alkaline NaOH conditions and that manganese in 
higher valences is capable of oxidizing I - to I2 under 
acid conditions H2SO4 thus the amount of I2 released is equivalent to the 
dissolved oxygen originally present. The iodine is measured with standard sodium 
thiosulfate Na2S2O3.5H2O solution and interpreted in terms of dissolved oxygen.
MnO2 + 2 I - + 2 H2SO4 ----> 
Mn2+ 
+ I2 + 2 H2O
Winkler Method
The reaction of winkler procedure is as follows:
Mn++ + 2OH - 
----> 
 Mn(OH)2
 White 
precipitate
If no oxygen is present ----> 
White precipitate of Mn(OH)2 
forms when MnSO4 and the alkali iodide reagent (NaOH+ KI) are added 
to the sample.
If oxygen is present in the sample then some of Mn2+ is 
oxidized to Mn4+ and precipitates as brown hydrated oxide . The 
reaction is usually represented as follows:
Mn++ + 2OH - + O2 ----> 
MnO2 + H2O
Mn(OH)2 + O2 ----> MnO2 
+ H2O
The oxidation of Mn2+ to MnO2 sometimes called fixation of 
oxygen, vigorous shaking of samples for at least 20 seconds is needed. After 
shaking, the samples for a time sufficient to allow all oxygen to react, the 
sulfuric acid is added and the sample is now ready for titration with 0.025 M thiosulfate. 
The liberated iodine which is equivalent to the dissolved 
oxygen is measured by titration with 0.025 M Na2S2O3.5H2O.Under the low pH condition, MnO2
oxidizes I - to produce I2.
MnO2 + 2 I - + 4H+ ----> 
Mn2+ 
+ I2 + 2 H2O
N.B. The sample should be stoppered and shaken for at least 10 seconds.
Interference
The unmodified winkler method is subjected to interference with different 
substance and specially the oxidizing agents such as nitrite and Fe3+ 
that are 
capable of oxidizing I- to I2 and produce results that are 
too high to obtain a permanent end point. The reactions involved may be represented as follow 
:
2NO2-+ 2 I- + 4H+ ----> 
I2 
+ N2O2 + 2 H2O
N2O2 + H2O + O2 
----> 2NO2- + 2H+
Nitrite interference may be easily overcome by the use of sodium azide NaN3, it is 
most convenient to incorporate the azide in the alkali-KI reagent.When 
sulfuric acid is added NO2- is destroyed and the following 
reaction occurs :
NaN3 + H+ ----> 
HN3 + Na+
HN3 + NO2 - + H+ 
---->
N2 
+ N2O + H2O
By this procedure nitrite interference is eliminated and the method of 
determination reactions retains the simplicity of the original winkler 
procedure.
Safety Precautions
The sample must be kept away from direct sunlight.
Make sure the sample bottle is correctly labeled.
Make sure the sample bottle is free from dust and organic 
 matter.
Tools and Equipment
Apparatus
One 300 ml BOD Bottle, Pipettes (2mL- 3mL- 5mL).
Reagents
Manganous Sulfate Solution-Dissolve 
 364g of manganous sulfate MnSO4.H2O in distilled 
 water, and dilute to1 liter.
Alkali-Iodide, 
 Azide Reagent-Dissolve 500g of sodium hydroxide NaOH and 135g NaI
 in distilled water and dilute to 1 liter. Add 10g NaN3 dissolved in 
 40mL distilled
 water
Sodium 
 ThioSulfate Standard Solution (0.025M)-Dissolve 6.025g of Na2S2O3.5H2O in distilled water. Standardize with Bi-Iodate solution.
Standard 
 Potassium Bi-Iodate Solution (0.0021M)-Dissolve 
 812.4mg KH(IO3)2 in distilled water, and dilute 
 to1 liter.
Starch Solution-
 Use either an aqueous solution or a soluble starch powder mixtures.
Sulfuric Acid -Concentrated 
 sulfuric acid H2SO4, one milliliter is equivalent to about 
 3mL Alkali-Iodide, Azide Reagent.
Standardization
Dissolve approximately 2g KI free from iodate in flask with 100mL to 150mL distilled water, add 1mL 
 (6N) H2SO4 or few drops of conc. H2SO4 
 and 20mL Standard Bi-Iodate solution.
Dilute to 200mL and titrate librated iodine with thiosulfate titrant adding 
 starch toward the end of titration when pale straw color is reached. If the solutions are of equal 
 strengths, 20mL (0.025M) Na2S2O3 is required, if not adjust the Na2S2O3 
 solution to (0.025M).
Work To be Carried Out
Procedure
Add 1mL MnSO4 solution to the sample 
collected in 250-300 mL bottle, followed by 1 mL alkali-iodide, 
 azide reagent if pipettes are dipped into sample rinse them before returning 
them to the reagent bottles. Hold pipette tip just above liquid surface 
when adding reagent.
Stopper carefully to exclude air bubbles
Mix by inverting bottle a few times. When 
precipitate has settled sufficiently to approximately half the bottle volume, 
to leave clear supernate above the manganese hydroxide floc.
Add 1mL conc. H2SO4.
Restopper and mix by inverting several times until 
dissolution is complete.
Take 100mL of the 
sample and titrate.
Titrate with 0.025M Na2S2O3 
solution to a pale straw color. Add a few drops of starch solution and continue 
titration to first disappearance of blue color.
Add 1mL MnSO4 solution to the sample 
collected in 250-300 mL bottle, followed by 1 mL alkali-iodide, 
 azide reagent if pipettes are dipped into sample rinse them before returning 
them to the reagent bottles. Hold pipette tip just above liquid surface 
when adding reagent.
Stopper carefully to exclude air bubbles
Mix by inverting bottle a few times. When 
precipitate has settled sufficiently to approximately half the bottle volume, 
to leave clear supernate above the manganese hydroxide floc.
Add 1mL conc. H2SO4.
Restopper and mix by inverting several times until 
dissolution is complete.
Take 100mL of the 
sample and titrate.
Titrate with 0.025M Na2S2O3 
solution to a pale straw color. Add a few drops of starch solution and continue 
titration to first disappearance of blue color.
Calculation
For titration 
of 100 mL sample, 1mL (0.025M) Na2S2O3 = 
2 mg DO/L
mg O2/L = V M 
 8 1000 / V1
Where:
M = Molarity of sodium thiosulfate,
V = Milliliter of Na2S2O3
 titrated,
8 = Equivalent Weight of O2 
 and
V1 = mL of sample (100).
